raw_case_text:
On 20 November 2016, a febrile, 25-year-old, 35-week pregnant woman was admitted for the fourth time during the pregnancy at Vanga Hospital, Vanga, DR Congo. She had sickle-cell disease, with a history of several crises over the years and two previous spontaneous abortions (in 2012 and 2014). She obtained a bednet at her first antenatal visit, and was followed thereafter. She took 5 mg folic acid daily, and received prophylactic doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in weeks 16 and 26. Overall, she was hospitalised thrice for malaria during the 1st, 2nd and 3rd trimester, and once during the 2nd trimester for a sickle-cell crisis (without malaria) and was treated with blood transfusion. The first malaria hospitalisation was at 12 weeks, followed by a sickle-cell crisis at 19 weeks, then malaria again at weeks 21 and 35. She was treated with 500 mg quinine twice daily for 7 days during the first two malaria episodes. Her thick and thin blood smears were malaria-negative after each course of treatment. She reported to use her bednet regularly, and our nurse verified the presence of the net at her home during the second hospitalisation. The physical exam upon her final admission revealed fever (38.9 C), an elevated respiratory rate (27 cycles/minute), and marginal hypotension (100/60 mmHg). Her palpebral and bulbar conjunctivae were pale and anicteric, respectively. The fundal height was 36 cm, foetal echocardiograms were normal, and no uterine contractions were detected. Her blood smears were positive for P. falciparum. The patient was stable overall. We administered 80/480 mg artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem ) for 3 days with 1000 mg paracetamol start and as needed for the fever. On the 5th day of admission, she went into active labour. During labour, both twins developed acute foetal distress, indicated by tachycardia. A C-section was promptly performed to save the babies. Their new-born exam results are in Table 1.
The mother was malaria-negative 7 days after treatment, but her twins had malaria at birth. They received 20 mg quinine intravenously twice daily, and 2 mg vitamin K intramuscularly for 2 days. However, on their third day of life, both developed fever but their blood smears were malaria-negative. A bacterial infection was suspected, as prematurity and LBW are commonly associated with neonatal infection. Both twins were prescribed a daily, 7-day long intravenous course of 200 mg ceftriaxone, besides quinine.
Fever in both twins quickly resolved, and twin-A totally recovered within 2 days of antibiotic treatment. Twin-B, however, who also had lymphocytosis, developed acute respiratory distress and hypoxia. Her oxygen saturation rapidly dropped from >90% to 60% in 2 hrs. Oxygen was given at 1 l/pm by nasal cannula to keep the saturation above 90%. The next day, she died of respiratory distress.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old pregnant female at 35 weeks gestation with sickle-cell disease presenting with fever, tachypnea, and marginal hypotension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old pregnant woman (35 weeks twin gestation) with known sickle-cell disease was admitted with acute fever. She had three previous hospitalizations during this pregnancy for malaria and sickle-cell crises. On hospital day 5, she went into active labor complicated by acute fetal distress (fetal tachycardia) in both twins, prompting emergency cesarean delivery. On day 3 of life, both twins developed fevers; Twin A recovered with antibiotics, while Twin B developed acute respiratory failure and hypoxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle-cell disease with recurrent crises; two previous spontaneous abortions (2012 and 2014). Hospitalized thrice for malaria (weeks 12, 21, and 35) and once for sickle-cell crisis with transfusion (week 19); treated with oral quinine (500 mg BID for 7 days) during first two malaria episodes with documented negative smears. Prophylaxis: Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in weeks 16 and 26, daily folic acid 5 mg, regular bednet use. Resident of Vanga, DR Congo.
subjective.review_of_systems: Acute fever, tachypnea; denies uterine contractions on initial admission.

objective.physical_examination: Mother: Febrile (38.9 °C), tachypneic (respiratory rate 27 breaths/min), blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Pale palpebral conjunctivae, anicteric sclerae. Fundal height 36 cm; normal fetal heart rates on admission; no uterine contractions. Twins: Preterm, low birth weight, developed intrapartum tachycardia; Twin B developed acute respiratory distress and severe hypoxia (SpO2 dropping from >90% to 60% in 2 hours).
objective.routine_investigations: Mother: Fetal echocardiograms normal on admission; repeat blood smear at day 7 postpartum was negative. Twins: Twin B demonstrated lymphocytosis. Repeat neonatal blood smears on day 3 of life were negative for hemoparasites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Gestational Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a woman with sickle-cell disease, resulting in preterm twin delivery and congenital Plasmodium falciparum malaria in both twins, complicated by fatal neonatal respiratory distress in Twin B. Maternal blood smears on admission were positive for Plasmodium falciparum. Both twins had blood smears positive for Plasmodium falciparum malaria at birth.
Plan & Outcome: Mother treated with oral artemether-lumefantrine (80/480 mg) for 3 days and paracetamol, achieving negative smears by day 7. Emergency C-section performed for intrapartum fetal distress. Both twins treated with intravenous quinine (20 mg BID) and intramuscular vitamin K for 2 days. On day 3, due to fever, intravenous ceftriaxone (200 mg daily for 7 days) was added for suspected neonatal sepsis. Twin A fully recovered in 2 days. Twin B developed refractory respiratory distress and hypoxia despite supplemental oxygen and died on day 4 of life.
